extracted.intended_audience: academic economists, empirical researchers, and policy analysts studying education policy and causal inference (impact evaluation) in developing-country contexts
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical impact-evaluation of a public primary-school construction program (SD INPRES) on the Islamic education sector using district- and village-level panel data, event studies, synthetic DID, heterogeneous-effects and selection-correction methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comprehensive administrative registries and complementary historical data
rubrics_metrics.description: Rely on newly compiled administrative data from MORA (universe of madrasa and pesantren active in 2019) and an analogous MEC registry of secular schools (219,145 schools) including establishment date, grade level, and private/public status; address potential concerns about survival bias using a triennial census of villages (Podes) beginning in 1980 and other historical administrative sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple data sources to validate patterns (e.g., Podes 1980–1993 to rule out survivor bias). Acknowledge coverage limitations (SIAP covers ~20% of madrasa; Susenas does not record informal pesantren attendance).

rubrics_metrics.name: District-level balanced-panel specification with fixed effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate a balanced panel at the district-year level: y_jt = θ_j + θ_t + β INPRES_jt + (X'_j θ_t)' η + ε_jt, where the outcome is the number of Islamic schools per 1,000 children and θ_j and θ_t are district and year fixed effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normalize outcomes (per 1,000 children in 1971). Include district and year FE to control for time-invariant district heterogeneity and common shocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control flexibly for INPRES targeting variables via interactions with year fixed effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Include INPRES targeting variables (1971 child population, school enrollment, concurrent water and sanitation program) and historical prevalence of Islamic schools (1959) interacted with year fixed effects to flexibly account for differential trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following Duflo (2001) logic, controlling for these interactions helps ensure estimated effects are not driven by time-varying correlates of the enrollment levels used to determine program eligibility; report that effects are conditional on initial enrollment/population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cluster standard errors at the policy-relevant aggregation level
rubrics_metrics.description: Cluster standard errors at the district level for district-panel estimates and at the village level for village-panel estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose clustering level consistent with treatment assignment and estimation unit to account for correlated shocks and inferential validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthetic Difference-in-Differences (SDID) to improve robustness to parallel-trends violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement SDID (Arkhangelsky et al., 2021) which reweights and matches pre-INPRES trends across high- and low-exposure districts to deliver estimates more robust than standard DID to parallel-trends violations. For implementation, discretize INPRES into a binary regressor (set INPRES_jt = 1 for districts above the 51st percentile in INPRES school construction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize SDID uses less continuous variation (due to discretization) but offers more compelling local comparisons where parallel trends are more plausible; report both standard DID and SDID results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event-study visualization and allowing coefficients to vary over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot event studies allowing β to vary by semi-decade (or by year) to visualize dynamic responses and identify a break in trends (e.g., mid-1970s increase in Islamic school entry in high-INPRES districts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use both graphical and estimation-based event studies to check for pre-trends and to describe timing and persistence of effects; complement visuals with formal sensitivity tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roth and Rambachan (2022) pre-trends sensitivity procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the Roth & Rambachan method that formalizes pre-trends testing by allowing uncertainty over the magnitude of true pre-period trends and computing confidence sets over how much post-intervention trends could depart from pre-trends before nullifying findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report how large a post-INPRES violation (parameter m) would need to be to invalidate results; interpret large required m as evidence findings are unlikely driven by non-parallel trends, while noting limits for continuous treatments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Village-level staggered-entry specification with fixed effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate a village-year specification: y_vt = θ_v + θ_t + Σ_{τ=-5}^{10} γ_τ INPRES_{v,t-τ} + (X'_v θ_t) η + ε_vt, where INPRES_{v,t-τ} are yearly indicators relative to the first SD INPRES built (τ=0), using a balanced panel from 1960–1999.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use village fixed effects and year FE, and interact predetermined village characteristics with year FE; this captures local, timing-based variation and complements district-level results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Borusyak et al. (2024) (or staggered-treatment-robust) estimator to allow arbitrary effect heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement the Borusyak et al. estimator: estimate fixed effects using untreated observations, impute untreated outcomes for treated observations, and compute γ_τ as weighted averages of actual minus imputed outcomes to address biases in staggered DID when treatment effects are heterogeneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This estimator reduces bias from treatment-timing heterogeneity. Present results alongside standard DID and show no evidence of pre-trends with this method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for endogenous timing by checking correlations between treatment timing and pre-treatment covariates
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate whether the timing of SD INPRES entry is correlated with 1972 presence of Islamic schools, predetermined agricultural productivity (potential crop yields), natural advantages (elevation, distance to the coast), and other pretreatment variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If timing is uncorrelated with these pre-treatment covariates, it supports plausibly exogenous timing; report balance tests (Appendix Table A.4) to reassure against endogenous timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and exploit heterogeneous funding capacity via interaction terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate heterogeneous effects by interacting INPRES with proxies for local funding capacity: rice yield (FAO-GAEZ median split) and waqf endowments (mosque land endowed as of 1960, median split).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct standardized/time-invariant proxies and interact them with treatment to test mechanisms (e.g., private financing channels); interpret stronger responses in high-waqf or high-rice-yield villages as evidence for mobilization-driven expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct outcomes carefully (per-capita normalization, curriculum shares, ideology proxies) and use retrospective panels when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Outcomes include number of Islamic schools per 1,000 children, mean curriculum subject shares (Islamic subjects, Pancasila/civic, Indonesian language) constructed from SIAP timetables using schools' establishment years to form district×grade×year retrospective panels, and standardized religious ideology predicted from school names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge data limits (SIAP covers ~20% of madrasa and secular schools do not report to SIAP); when only cross-sectional curriculum snapshots exist, build retrospective panels using establishment dates but discuss assumptions and potential reporting selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use penalized regression (ridge) on school-name text to predict religious ideology
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify common words/acronyms in Islamic school names, regress observed curriculum hours or Islamic-subject shares on name-word dummies (interacted with level and province), select covariates using ridge shrinkage, and predict ideology for schools lacking curriculum data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use penalization to avoid overfitting; validate predicted ideology against observed curriculum where available and use as a robustness check for curriculum-differentiation conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess formalization by tracking composition changes (madrasa vs pesantren/diniyah) over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare shares of madrasa entrants to informal pesantren/diniyah entrants across markets and time to detect formalization of the Islamic sector following SD INPRES (e.g., rising madrasa share among entrants in early 1980s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report aggregate shares and entry rates; interpret shifts toward madrasa as increased formalization enabling grade progression and switching between public and religious schools. Use Appendix tables/figures to corroborate patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness checks across windows, estimators, and controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Run robustness analyses: shorter panel windows (e.g., 1968–83), remove time-varying controls, use different clustering, exclude certain observations, and compare standard DID, SDID, and Borusyak estimators; report that core results hold across these checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document sensitivity to specification choices and present alternative estimates in appendices (e.g., Appendix Table A.5, A.7–A.9, Figures A.1–A.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Address survivor and attrition bias explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that increased Islamic school entry after the 1970s can be seen in historical administrative data (Podes 1980/1983/1990/1993) not subject to attrition inherent to contemporary registries, mitigating concerns that 2019 registry patterns reflect differential survival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use independent historical data sources to validate registry-based findings; present appendix tables demonstrating consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret substitution and complementarity via within-market correlation analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine whether newly entering Islamic schools are built in villages with/without corresponding public or non-Islamic private school entry (e.g., 86% of MD entering 1973–78 were built in villages without any MI construction) and compute correlations between subsequent construction across sectors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use share and correlation statistics to characterize whether sectors compete head-on or expand in distinct markets; provide correlation magnitudes and contextual interpretation (e.g., low correlation suggests distinct markets and excess demand).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection-correction for schooling attainment outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for selection into continued education when estimating Islamic graduation shares using parametric (Heckman 1976) and semiparametric (Newey 2009) procedures: first-stage model completion probability; second-stage model Islamic completion including selection-correction term; use an exclusion restriction (exposure to a pilot compulsory schooling program in the 1960s) that shifts completion but not Islamic choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report both unadjusted and selection-adjusted estimates, show similar signs/magnitudes to argue selection does not drive main results, and justify the exclusion restriction empirically (Appendix Table A.20).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for measurement and reporting limitations in surveys
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that Susenas reports madrasa vs secular education only at highest attainment level and does not record informal pesantren; use IFLS for validation although it has limited geographic scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple survey sources where possible, interpret results in light of measurement limitations, and perform robustness checks using alternative data (IFLS) when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret curriculum substitution effects accounting for changes in total instruction hours
rubrics_metrics.description: When finding increases in Islamic/Arabic instruction shares, consider whether these reflect substitution away from Pancasila/Indonesian instruction or increases in total instruction hours (e.g., primary level often subsumes subjects under 'thematic' blocks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report both shares and total instruction hours (Appendix Table A.12) and discuss plausible mechanisms (e.g., accommodation via longer school days or reallocation across subjects).
